'''Sir David Anthony King''' (born 12 August 1939)<ref name=whoswho/> is a South African-born British [[chemist]], academic, and head of the [[Climate Crisis Advisory Group]] (CCAG).

King first taught at [[Imperial College, London]], the [[University of East Anglia]], and was then Brunner Professor of Physical Chemistry (1974–1988) at the [[University of Liverpool]]. He held the [[1920 Chair of Physical Chemistry]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] from 1988 to 2006, and was [[Master (college)|Master]] of [[Downing College, Cambridge]], from 1995 to 2000: he is now [[emeritus professor]]. While at Cambridge, he was successively a [[Fellow (Oxbridge)|fellow]] of [[St John's College, Cambridge|St John's College]], Downing College, and [[Queens' College, Cambridge|Queens' College]]. Moving to the [[University of Oxford]], he was Director of the [[Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment]] from 2008 to 2012, and a Fellow of [[University College, Oxford]], from 2009 to 2012. He was additionally President of [[Collegio Carlo Alberto]] in Turin, Italy (2008–2011), and [[Chancellor (education)|Chancellor]] of the University of Liverpool (2010–2013).

Outside of academia, King was [[Government Chief Scientific Adviser (United Kingdom)|Chief Scientific Adviser]] to the UK Government and Head of the [[Government Office for Science]] from 2000 to 2007. He was then senior scientific adviser to [[UBS]], a Swiss investment bank and financial services company, from 2008 to 2013. From 2013 to 2017, he returned to working with the UK Government as Special Representative for Climate Change to the [[Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs|Foreign Secretary]]. He was also Chairman of the government's [[Future Cities Catapult]] from 2013 to 2016.

==Early life and education==
King was born on 12 August 1939 in South Africa, son of Arnold Tom Wallis King, of Johannesburg, director of a paint company, and Patricia Mary Bede, née Vardy.<ref>People of Today, Debrett's Peerage Ltd, 2006, p. 912</ref><ref>The International Who's Who 1992-3, Europa Publications, 1992, p. 869</ref><ref>Beerman's Financial Year Book of Southern Africa- Investors' Manual and Cyclopaedia of South African Public Companies 1973, Combined Publishers, p. 429</ref> His elder brother, Michael Wallis King (born 1937), was director of the [[FirstRand]] bank and vice-chair of the multinational mining company [[Anglo American plc]].<ref>Who's Who of Southern Africa, Argus Printing and Publishing Co., 2003, p. 170</ref> King was educated at [[St John's College, Johannesburg|St John's College]], an all-boys private school in [[Johannesburg]]. He studied at [[University of the Witwatersrand]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) degree and then a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (PhD) degree in 1963.<ref name="WW 21">{{cite web |title=King, Sir David (Anthony), (born 12 Aug. 1939), Director, Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, University of Oxford, 2008–12; Fellow, University College, Oxford, 2009–12; Chief Scientific Adviser to the Government, and Head, Government Office for Science (formerly Office of Science and Technology, then of Science and Innovation), 2000–07; Executive Chair, Centre for Climate Repair, Cambridge, since 2019 |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U23112 |website=[[Who's Who 2021]] |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |date=1 December 2020}}</ref>

==Academic career==
After his PhD, King moved to the United Kingdom where he was a Shell Scholar at Imperial College, London, from 1963 to 1966.<ref name="WW 21" /> He was then a [[lecturer]] in the School of Chemical Sciences of the University of East Anglia from 1966 to 1974.<ref name="WW 21" /><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = King | first1 = D. | last2 = Wells | first2 = M. | title = Molecular beam investigation of adsorption kinetics on bulk metal targets: Nitrogen on tungsten | journal = Surface Science | volume = 29 | issue = 2 | pages = 454–482 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.1016/0039-6028(72)90232-4| bibcode = 1972SurSc..29..454K }}</ref> He was appointed Brunner Professor of [[Physical Chemistry]] at the University of Liverpool in 1974. He was a member of the National Executive of the [[Association of University Teachers]] from 1970 until 1978, and served as its president for the 1976/77 academic year.<ref name="WW 21" />

In 1988, King was appointed 1920 Professor of Physical Chemistry at the University of Cambridge. He subsequently served as Head of the [[Yusuf Hamied Department of Chemistry|University's Department of Chemistry]] from 1993 to 2000, and was its director of research from 2005 to 2011. When he first moved to Cambridge in 1988, he was elected a [[Fellow (Oxbridge)|Fellow]] of St John's College, Cambridge. He moved from St John's when he was elected Master of Downing College, Cambridge, in 1995. He stepped down as Master in 2000, and was then a Fellow of Queens' College, Cambridge, from 2001 to 2008.<ref name="WW 21" />

From 2008 to 2012, King was Director of the Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment at the University of Oxford.<ref name=whoswho/> He was also a Fellow of University College, Oxford, from 2009 to 2012.<ref name="WW 21" /> He was President of Collegio Carlo Alberto in Turin, Italy, from 2008 to 2011,<ref name="WW 21" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Collegio Aperto: Sir David King |url=https://www.carloalberto.org/event/david-king/ |website=Collegio Carlo Alberto |access-date=13 April 2021 |date=23 October 2009}}</ref> and was Chancellor of the University of Liverpool from 2010 to 2013.<ref name="WW 21" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.liv.ac.uk/news/press_releases/2009/11/sir-david-king-appointed-liverpool-chancellor.htm|title=Home - News - University of Liverpool|website=liv.ac.uk|language=en|access-date=25 January 2018}}</ref>

===Research===
King has published over 500 papers on his research in chemical physics and on science and policy.<ref name=whoswho/><ref name="GOV bio" />

During his time at Cambridge, King had, together with [[Gabor A. Somorjai|Gabor Somorjai]] and [[Gerhard Ertl]], shaped the discipline of [[surface science]] and helped to explain the underlying principles of [[heterogeneous catalysis]]. However, the 2007 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] was awarded to Ertl alone.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/science/science-news/3310155/Nobel-prize-for-superficial-work.html|title=Nobel prize for superficial work|first=Roger|last=Highfield|date=11 October 2007|via=telegraph.co.uk}}</ref>

==Career outside academia==
King was the Chief Scientific Adviser to the UK Government and Head of the [[Government Office for Science]] from October 2000 to 31 December 2007, under prime ministers [[Tony Blair]] and [[Gordon Brown]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = King | first1 = D. A. | title = The scientific impact of nations | doi = 10.1038/430311a | journal = Nature | volume = 430 | issue = 6997 | pages = 311–316 | year = 2004 | pmid = 15254529 | bibcode = 2004Natur.430..311K | doi-access = free }}</ref> In that time, he raised the profile of the need for governments to act on [[climate change]] and was instrumental in creating the £1 billion [[Energy Technologies Institute]]. In 2008 he co-authored ''The Hot Topic'' on this subject.<ref name=hottopic>{{cite book |last= King |first= David A. |author2=Gabrielle Walker |title= The Hot Topic |publisher= [[Bloomsbury Publishing]] |date=February 2008 |isbn= 978-0747593959 }}</ref>

During his tenure as Chief Scientific Adviser, he raised public awareness for climate change and initiated several foresight studies. As director of the government's Foresight Programme, he created an in-depth [[horizon scanning]] process which advised government on a wide range of long-term issues, from flooding to obesity.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = King | first1 = D. | title = Foresight report on obesity | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(07)61739-5 | journal = The Lancet | volume = 370 | issue = 9601 | pages = 1754 | year = 2007 | pmid = 18037076 | s2cid = 32777266 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = King | first1 = D. A. | last2 = Thomas | first2 = S. M. | doi = 10.1038/449791a | title = Big lessons for a healthy future | journal = Nature | volume = 449 | issue = 7164 | pages = 791–792 | year = 2007 | pmid =17943108| bibcode = 2007Natur.449..791K | doi-access = free }}</ref>  He also chaired the government's Global Science and Innovation Forum from its inception. King advised the government on issues including: [[2001 United Kingdom foot-and-mouth crisis|the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic 2001]]; post 9/11 risks to the UK; [[Genetically modified food|GM foods]]; energy provision; and innovation and wealth creation. He was heavily involved in the government's Science and Innovation Strategy 2004–2014. He suggested that scientists should honour a [[Hippocratic Oath for Scientists]].{{Citation needed|date=November 2020}}

In April 2008, King joined UBS, a Swiss investment bank, as senior science advisor.<ref name="WW 21" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://uk.reuters.com/article/idUKL114218920080411|title=UBS hires former UK chief science adviser|last=((Reuters Staff))|work=Reuters|access-date=21 November 2017|language=en-GB|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201182930/https://uk.reuters.com/article/uk-bank-climate/ubs-hires-former-uk-chief-science-adviser-idUKL114218920080411|archive-date=1 December 2017}}</ref> He left UBS to return to the UK government when he was appointed the Foreign Secretary's Special Representative for Climate Change in September 2013.<ref name="GOV bio">{{Cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/people/david-king|title=Sir David King |website=GOV.UK |language=en|access-date=21 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/foreign-secretarys-new-special-representative-for-climate-change|title=Foreign Secretary's new Special Representative for Climate Change - GOV.UK|website=gov.uk|language=en|access-date=21 November 2017}}</ref>

From 2013 to 2016, King was the first chairman of the Future Cities Catapult, a government-funded body conducting research into [[smart cities]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Multi-million pound future cities catapult to be hosted in London|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/multi-million-pound-future-cities-catapult-to-be-hosted-in-london|access-date=9 January 2020|website=GOV.UK|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://futurecities.catapult.org.uk/people/-/asset_publisher/zQ6NnjOqc7TQ/content/professor-sir-david-king |title=Future Cities - Professor Sir David King - People |access-date=1 November 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141101032933/https://futurecities.catapult.org.uk/people/-/asset_publisher/zQ6NnjOqc7TQ/content/professor-sir-david-king |archive-date=1 November 2014}}</ref>

In May 2020, in response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|COVID-19 pandemic]], King formed and led [[Independent SAGE]], a committee of unpaid experts which acts as a "shadow" of the UK government's [[Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies|SAGE]] group to address concerns of lack of transparency and political influence on that body.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Stone|first=Jon|date=3 May 2020|title=Top scientists set up 'shadow' SAGE committee to advise government amid concerns over political interference|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/coronavirus-sage-dominic-cummings-david-king-a9496546.html|access-date=24 November 2020|website=The Independent|language=en}}</ref>

== Views ==

=== Climate change ===
In his role as scientific advisor to the UK government King was outspoken on the subject of climate change, saying "''I see climate change as the greatest challenges facing Britain and the World in the 21st century''" <ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.coolkidsforacoolclimate.com/Climate%20Change%20News/David%20King.htm |title=The Challenge of Climate Change by Sir David King |access-date=13 October 2004 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040805205749/http://www.coolkidsforacoolclimate.com/Climate%20Change%20News/David%20King.htm |archive-date=5 August 2004}}</ref> and "''climate change is the most severe problem we are facing today – more serious even than the threat of terrorism''".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/|archive-url=https://swap.stanford.edu/20081217070228/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 December 2008|title=News|date=15 March 2016|work=The Telegraph|access-date=21 November 2017|language=en-GB|issn=0307-1235}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/3381425.stm|title=Global warming 'biggest threat'|date=2004|access-date=21 November 2017|language=en-GB}}</ref>

He strongly supports the work of the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]], saying in 2004 that the [[IPCC Third Assessment Report|2001 synthesis report]] "''is the best current statement on the state of play of the science of climate change, and that really does represent 1,000 scientists''".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200304/cmselect/cmenvaud/490/4033005.htm|title=House of Commons - Environmental Audit - Minutes of Evidence|last=Commons|first=The Committee Office, House of|website=publications.parliament.uk|access-date=21 November 2017}}</ref>

King criticised the [[Presidency of George W. Bush|Bush administration]] for what he saw as its failures in climate change policy, saying it is "''failing to take up the challenge of global warming"''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/3381425.stm|title=Global warming 'biggest threat'|date=2004|access-date=21 November 2017|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 2004, King gave evidence to a House of Commons [[Environmental Audit Select Committee|select committee]] confirming his view that "on a global and geological scale that climate change is the most serious problem we are faced with this century", and illustrated it with  a statement that "Fifty-five million years ago was a time when there was no ice on the earth; the Antarctic was the most habitable place for mammals".<ref>{{cite web|publisher=House of Commons|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200304/cmselect/cmenvaud/490/4033002.htm|date=30 March 2004|author=Environmental Audit Select Committee|title=Minutes of Evidence|access-date=15 December 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Ofcom|url=https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0030/45489/issue114.pdf|title=Ofcom Broadcast Bulletin 114|date=21 July 2008|accessdate=15 December 2022}}</ref> The ''[[Independent on Sunday]]'' reported that King had at a later event compared current and projected carbon dioxide levels with the record over the past 60 million years, and in an indirect quote suggested King implied that Antarctica was likely to be the world's "only" habitable continent by the end of this century if global warming remains unchecked.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/why-antarctica-will-soon-be-the-only-place-to-live-literally-58574.html |first = Geoffrey|last = Lean|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100817023019/http://www.independent.co.uk/environment/why-antarctica-will-soon-be-the-ionlyi-place-to-live--literally-561947.html |url-status=live|archive-date= 17 August 2010 | title=Why Antarctica will soon be the only place to live-literally|date=2 May 2004|work=The Independent on Sunday|access-date=15 December 2022|language=en-GB}}</ref> At the end of the 2007 programme "[[The Great Global Warming Swindle]]", broadcast on [[Channel 4]], [[Fred Singer]] ridiculed the reported view of the "chief scientist"; King's complaint to [[Ofcom]] that the programme was unfair and had not given a chance to clarify was upheld, despite Channel 4's arguments that King was not named and had not challenged earlier reporting.<ref>{{cite news|newspaper=The Guardian|date= 21 Jul 2008|first= David|last = Adam|title=Global warming documentary: The Ofcom report at a glance|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2008/jul/21/climatechange.carbonemissions|access-date=15 December 2022}}</ref>

King became head of the Climate Crisis Advisory Group in 2021, basing public meetings on a similar format to Independent SAGE, and publishing reports advising emission cuts and [[carbon dioxide removal]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.edie.net/climate-crisis-advisory-group-new-body-launches-modelled-after-british-scientists-covid-19-initiative/|author=Edie|date=21 June 2021|title=Climate Crisis Advisory Group: New body launches, modelled after British scientists’ Covid-19 initiative|access-date=15 December 2022}}</ref> He promotes the CCAG's 4R planet pathway: ''Reducing'' emissions; ''Removing'' the excess [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]] (GHGs) already in the atmosphere; ''Repairing'' ecosystems; strengthening local and global ''Resilience'' against inevitable climate impacts.<ref>{{Cite news |last=King |first=David |date=2024-05-27 |title=Humanity’s survival is still within our grasp – just. But only if we take these radical steps |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/article/2024/may/27/humanity-survival-emissions-resilience-ecosystems-greenhouse-gases |access-date=2024-05-30 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=About {{!}} Climate Crisis Advisory Group |url=https://www.ccag.earth/about#:~:text=Our%204R%20Planet%20Strategy |access-date=2024-05-30 |website=www.ccag.earth |language=en}}</ref>

=== Food production ===
King told ''The Independent'' newspaper in February 2007 "he agreed that organic food was no safer than chemically-treated food" and openly supported a study by the [[Manchester Business School]] that implicated [[organic farming]] practices in unfavourable CO<sub>2</sub> comparisons with conventional chemical farming.

In an article published in ''The Guardian'' in February 2009, King is quoted as saying that "future historians might look back on our particular recent past and see the Iraq war as the first of the conflicts of this kind – the first of the resource wars" and that this was "certainly the view" (that the invasion was motivated by a desire to secure energy supplies) he held at the time of the invasion, along with "quite a few people in government".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2009/feb/13/resource-wars-david-king|title=UK's ex-science chief predicts century of 'resource' wars|last=Randerson|first=James|date=13 February 2009|work=The Guardian|access-date=21 November 2017|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Energy ===
King is a strong supporter of [[nuclear power|nuclear electricity generation]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.smithschool.ox.ac.uk/a-low-carbon-nuclear-future-economic-assessment-of-nuclear-materials-and-spent-nuclear-fuel-management-in-the-uk/ |title=A low carbon nuclear future: Economic assessment of nuclear materials and spent nuclear fuel management in the UK : Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment |access-date=17 November 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110828063608/http://www.smithschool.ox.ac.uk/a-low-carbon-nuclear-future-economic-assessment-of-nuclear-materials-and-spent-nuclear-fuel-management-in-the-uk/ |archive-date=28 August 2011}}</ref> arguing that it is a safe, technically feasible solution that can help to reduce emissions from the utilities sector now, while the development of alternative low-carbon solutions is incentivised.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2005/dec/16/greenpolitics.environment|title=David King: The nuclear option is scientific necessity|last=King|first=David|date=16 December 2005|work=The Guardian|access-date=21 November 2017|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> In the transport sector, King has warned governments that conventional oil resources are more scarce than they believe and that [[peak oil]] might approach sooner than expected.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Owen | first1 = N. A. | last2 = Inderwildi | first2 = O. R. | last3 = King | first3 = D. A. | doi = 10.1016/j.enpol.2010.02.026 | title = The status of conventional world oil reserves—Hype or cause for concern? | journal = Energy Policy | volume = 38 | issue = 8 | pages = 4743–4749 | year = 2010 }}</ref> Moreover, he has criticised [[first generation biofuels]] due to the effect on [[food prices]] and subsequent effect on the developing world. He strongly supports [[second generation biofuels]], however, which are manufactured from inedible biomass such as [[corn stover]], wood chips or straw. These biofuels are not made from food sources<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Inderwildi | first1 = O. R. | last2 = King | first2 = D. A. | doi = 10.1039/b822951c | title = Quo vadis biofuels? | journal = Energy & Environmental Science | volume = 2 | issue = 4 | pages = 343 | year = 2009 }}</ref> (see [[food vs fuel]]).

King is a member of the [[Global Apollo Programme]] and headed its public launch in 2015. The programme calls for multinational research into reducing the cost of low-carbon electricity generation.

=== Humanism ===

King is a Distinguished Supporter of [[Humanists UK]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Distinguished supporters of Humanism Richard Norman and Colin Blakemore support H4BW |url=https://humanists.uk/2011/04/26/distinguished-supporters-of-humanism-richard-norman-and-colin-blakemore-support-h4bw/ |access-date=2022-11-22 |website=Humanists UK |language=en}}</ref>

=== Covid response ===

In July 2020 King advocated for school closures in the UK until covid cases were reduced to 1 in a million.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-QRhwcVMTZI&t=3678s&ab_channel=indie_SAGE | title=Independent SAGE - 14.07.20 | website=[[YouTube]] }}</ref>

== Honours and awards ==
King was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in the [[2003 New Year Honours|2003 New Year honours]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=15 August 2003|title=Honours and Awards|url=https://www.thegazette.co.uk/notice/L-57030-1003|access-date=24 November 2020|website=[[London Gazette]]}}</ref> In 2009, he was made a Chevalier of the [[Légion d'honneur|Légion d'Honneur]] by the French government.<ref name="GOV bio" />

In 1991 he received the BVC Medal and Prize, awarded by [[the British Vacuum Council]].{{Citation needed|date=November 2020}} He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1991,<ref>{{Cite web|title=David King|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/david-king-11748/|access-date=24 November 2020|website=Royal Society|language=en-gb}}</ref> a Foreign Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2002,<ref name="GOV bio" /> and an Honorary [[Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering]] (HonFREng) in 2006.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|title=List of Fellows|url=http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows?fa=k|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160326131201/http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows?fa=k|archive-date=26 March 2016|website=Royal Academy of Engineering}}</ref>

== In media ==
King appears in the film ''[[The Age of Stupid]]'', released in February 2009, talking about [[Hurricane Katrina]]. He was portrayed by [[David Calder (actor)|David Calder]] in the 2021 [[BBC]] television film ''[[The Trick (2021 film)|The Trick]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Trick |url=https://www.radiotimes.com/programme/b-f1oxgx/the-trick/ |website=[[Radio Times]] |access-date=20 October 2022 |archive-date=20 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221020093951/https://www.radiotimes.com/programme/b-f1oxgx/the-trick/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life==
By his first marriage, which ended in divorce, King has two sons. In 1983, he married, secondly, charity administrator and former head of a commercial law team,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jane Lichtenstein:'I wasn't trying to escape' |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/features/3636460/Jane-LichtensteinI-wasnt-trying-to-escape.html |access-date=22 November 2022|website=telegraph.co.uk}}</ref> Jane Margaret, daughter of [[general practitioner]] Hans Eugen Lichtenstein, [[Order_of_the_British_Empire#Current_classes|OBE]],<ref>{{Cite web|date=14 June 2002|title=Order of the British Empire, Civil |url=http://www.theguardian.com/uk/2002/jun/15/monarchy.politics14 |access-date=22 November 2022 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}</ref> of [[Llandrindod Wells]], [[Powys]], Wales, a Holocaust survivor from a family that owned leather goods shops and an umbrella factory in [[Berlin]]. They have a son and a daughter.<ref>"People of Today", Debrett's Peerage Ltd, 2006, p. 912</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lichtenstein |first=Jonathan |date=2 April 2019|title=Hans Lichtenstein obituary |url=http://www.theguardian.com/society/2019/apr/02/hans-lichtenstein-obituary |access-date=22 November 2022 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}</ref>
